subject: Diagnosing large standard errors – any lessons?

messages.author: 9044165ad6889125
messages.subject: Diagnosing large standard errors – any lessons?
parts:
Hi,

I'm trying to understand why a particular model has large standard errors. The population model is a bifactor model. Syntax is below:

pop <- ' 
  # define two substantive factors with standardized loadings
  c1 =~ 0.570*x1 + 0.632*x2 + 0.744*x3 + 0.543*x4
  c2 =~ 0.570*x5 + 0.632*x6 + 0.744*x7 + 0.543*x8
  
  # define a single ULMC 
  m1 =~ .271*x1 + .316*x2 + .374*x3 + .3000*x4 + .374*x5 + .3000*x6 + .271*x7 + .316*x8 

  # define a relationship linking substantive factors
  c1 ~~ 0.2*c2
  
  # substantive factors standardized
  c1 ~~ 1*c1
  c2 ~~ 1*c2
  
  # method factor standardized
  m1 ~~ 1*m1
  
  # method factors are not correlated with substantive factors
  c1 ~ 0*m1
  c2 ~ 0*m1
   
  # error variances for substantive factors
  x1 ~~ 0.602*x1
  x2 ~~ 0.501*x2
  x3 ~~ 0.307*x3
  x4 ~~ 0.615*x4
  x5 ~~ 0.535*x5
  x6 ~~ 0.511*x6
  x7 ~~ 0.373*x7
  x8 ~~ 0.605*x8
'
...which I've used to generate an implied covariance matrix.

cov <- fitted(sem(pop))
cov <- cov[["cov"]]

When I fit an estimating model that recovers the parameters, I only can get small standard errors at unusually high sample sizes (n > 1,000,000). 

est <- ' 
  # define a single ULMC 
  m1 =~ x8 + x7 + x6 + x5 + x4 + x3 + x2 + x1 
  
  # define three substantive factors with standardized loadings
  c2 =~ x5 + x6 + x7 + x8
  c1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4

  # define a relationship linking substantive factors
  c1 ~~ c2
'
fit <- cfa(est, sample.cov = cov, sample.nobs = 100, std.lv = TRUE, orthogonal=TRUE) 

I'm trying to understand why this is the case. 

Chris

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Diagnosing large standard errors – any lessons?
parts: I only can get small standard errors at unusually high sample sizes (n > 1,000,000).

You haven't stated your criterion for what is a small SE.  But you don't have a lot of items to justify estimating both a factor correlation and what you call the ULMC loadings.  Bifactor models are typically orthogonal, and that single parameter could affect your SEs a lot.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

Thanks for responding, Terrence. I always appreciate your help.

Yes, the bifactor is orthogonal in this case. 

By small, I’m thinking within the range of .05-.01…intuitively. The ULMC loadings are also small (~.3).

Could you clarify or point me to a reference that explains why an orthogonal bifactor has such a profound impact on the SEs?

Chris

messages.author: b8fd92e5e3662745
messages.subject: Re: Diagnosing large standard errors – any lessons?
parts:
I think intuitively, you are saying that the first substantive factor is approximately a sum of items with the same weight (of about 0.5 to 0.6), AND the second substantive factor is approximately a sum of items with the same weight (of about 0.5 to 0.6, AND the  methods factor is approximately a sum of items with the same weight (of about 0.3). You end up with a correlation matrix that has a rather weak structure, and teasing out if say high values of x1 and x2 together are attributable to the substantive factor or to the methods factor is nigh impossible. Put differently, while your model is nominally identified by all rules, it lacks empirical identification. If your methods factor has a mix of pluses and minuses, especially within the same factor, you would get "small" standard errors much easier: if the method factor has opposite signs on x1 and x2, then eventually we'd see that jointly high values of x1 and x2 really mean something for the substantive factor only.

If you simplify the model way further, and leave only four parameters (substantive factor variances set to one; the four parameters are: (1) factor correlation; (2) the substantive factor loadings assumed the same; (3) the method factor loadings assumed the same; (4) the unique variances assumed the same), you can obtain the implied matrix, plug it into the likelihood, and obtain the derivatives/the information matrix to see how poorly this model works in practice. That would be a useful exercise for a math strong grad student.

Chris
